name: IVFFlat Index
question: Can I search only the nearest clusters?
summary: IVF (inverted file) indexing groups vectors into clusters with k-means, each represented by a centroid. A query is first compared with the centroids, then only the vectors in the closest few clusters (the probes) are scanned. “Flat” means vectors inside each list are stored uncompressed, so distances within a list are exact.
useCases: Moderate datasets where fast index builds matter
Postgres with pgvector, when memory is tight
Batch-loaded data that doesn’t change much

items.detail: number of clusters; pgvector suggests rows ÷ 1,000 up to 1M rows, √rows above
clusters scanned per query; higher = better recall, slower
k-means runs on the data present when the index is built
compress vectors inside lists to save memory

steps: Load representative data before building, since clusters are learned from it
Set lists to about rows ÷ 1,000 (up to 1M rows) or √rows beyond that
Start probes around √lists and tune for your recall target
Rebuild the index after large changes to the data
pitfalls: An index built on an empty or tiny table has poor clusters
Recall drops as new data drifts from the original clusters
Queries near cluster borders need more probes
caption: Faded clusters are never scanned. Raising probes trades speed for recall.

code.text: faiss.normalize_L2(xb)            # unit length: inner product = cosine
index.add(xb)                     # each vector joins its nearest centroid's list
xq = embed(["How do I reset my UPI PIN?"]).astype("float32")
D, I = index.search(xq, 10)       # exact distances inside ~45 of 2,000 lists
exact = faiss.IndexFlatIP(d)      # brute force, for evaluation only

steps.title: Load and normalise the vectors
steps.text: Load representative data first, because the clusters are learned from it. Unit-length vectors make inner product equal to cosine similarity.

steps.title: Train the centroids
steps.text: k-means on a sample learns nlist centroids. Two million rows ÷ 1,000 gives 2,000 lists; the picture uses 4.

steps.title: Fill the inverted lists
steps.text: Every vector is stored in the list of its nearest centroid. A list is scanned as a unit at query time.

steps.title: Pick the nearest lists
steps.text: The query is compared with every centroid, a cheap step, and the nprobe closest lists are chosen: 2 of 4 here.

steps.title: Scan only those lists
steps.text: Exact distances are computed inside the probed lists only: 16 of 32 vectors here, and 45 of 2,000 lists, about 2%, at full scale.

steps.title: Measure recall
steps.text: Compare with exact search on sample queries. If recall@10 is below target, raise nprobe; if it falls as data changes, rebuild.

pros: Fast index builds and modest memory
Two predictable knobs: lists and probes
probes can change per query with no rebuild
Pairs with product quantization (IVF-PQ) for large corpora
cons: Needs representative data before the index is built
Recall degrades as new data drifts from the trained centroids
Usually lower recall than HNSW at the same latency
Queries near cluster borders need more probes
avoidWhen: Data arrives continuously and shifts over time (HNSW needs no training)
Hundreds of millions of vectors on one machine with little RAM (DiskANN or IVF-PQ)

playgroundGuide.scenario: A payments company's help centre stores its article chunks in Postgres with an IVFFlat index. Below is a scaled-down copy: 800 vectors in 8 topic clusters and 40 test queries. You choose how many lists k-means creates and how many of them each query scans, then compare the results with exact search.
controls: Pick the number of lists (clusters) the index is built with.
Drag probes to set how many of the nearest lists each query scans.
Tick “build on the first 10% of rows” to see an index trained before most data arrived.

outputs.name: Recall@10
outputs.meaning: Share of the true 10 nearest neighbours the index returns, averaged over 40 queries.

outputs.name: Vectors scanned
outputs.meaning: Vectors in the probed lists ÷ all 800. The main cost of an IVF query.

outputs.name: Work saved vs exact search
outputs.meaning: How many times fewer distances than scanning every vector.

outputs.name: Largest list
outputs.meaning: Share of all vectors in the biggest list. Balanced lists keep query cost predictable.

presets.name: Starting index
presets.expect: 16 lists, 1 probe: 83% recall while scanning 6% of the vectors, about 16× less work than exact search.

presets.name: Tuned
presets.expect: 32 lists, 3 probes: 99% recall while scanning 9% of the vectors.

presets.name: Built too early
presets.expect: Trained on the first 80 rows only: the largest list holds 46% of the data, so 2 probes scan 41% of the vectors to reach 98% recall.

presets.name: Many small lists
presets.expect: 64 lists, 2 probes: only 3% scanned, but recall falls to 86%.

missions.text: Reach at least 97% recall while scanning no more than 10% of the vectors.
missions.hint: Use more, smaller lists and 3 or more probes.

missions.text: Keep probes at 2 and find a number of lists that drops recall below 90%.
missions.hint: More lists means each one is smaller, so 2 probes cover less of the space.

missions.text: Build the index on early data and make one list hold at least 40% of all vectors.
missions.hint: Tick the first-10% box; 16 lists shows it clearly.

tools.best: IVFFlat and HNSW indexes inside Postgres, queried with plain SQL next to your other tables.

cons: Index must be built after data is loaded
Very large collections need careful tuning and hardware

goals: Explain how lists and probes trade recall for speed
Set lists and a starting probes value from the row count
Recognise when an IVF index needs rebuilding

practice.scenario: A fintech keeps 2 million support-article chunks in Postgres. An IVFFlat index with 2,000 lists (rows ÷ 1,000) builds in minutes, and setting probes to about 45 (√lists) gives the recall they need, without adding a separate vector database.

industries.use: Add semantic search without running a new database
Product indexes rebuilt nightly from fresh data
Similarity search over batch-loaded event embeddings

practice.analogy: A library organised into sections. To find a book, you walk to the two most likely sections and ignore the rest.

library.name: pgvector
library.what: The Postgres extension for vectors. Supports IVFFlat and HNSW indexes alongside your normal tables and SQL.

samples.code:
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  body      text,
  embedding vector(384)
);

-- Build AFTER loading data: clusters are learned from existing rows
CREATE INDEX ON chunks USING ivfflat (embedding vector_cosine_ops)
  WITH (lists = 2000);                  -- ≈ rows / 1000 for 2M rows

SET ivfflat.probes = 45;                -- ≈ √lists; raise for better recall

SELECT id, body
FROM chunks
ORDER BY embedding <=> $1               -- cosine distance to the query vector
LIMIT 5;

numericDrill.question: A pgvector table has 600,000 rows. What value of lists does pgvector suggest?
numericDrill.answer: Up to 1M rows, lists ≈ rows ÷ 1,000 = 600. Start probes around √600 ≈ 24 and tune for recall.

interview.question: How does IVF trade recall for speed?
interview.answer: It scans only the closest few clusters (probes) instead of every vector. More probes raise recall and latency; a true neighbour in an unscanned cluster is missed.

interview.question: When would you choose IVFFlat over HNSW?
interview.answer: When you need faster index builds and less memory, or rebuild from batch data regularly, and can accept slightly lower recall at the same speed. HNSW is usually better for low-latency, high-recall search.

mistakes.mistake: Building the index before loading data

mistakes.fix: Rebuild when the data distribution drifts

quiz.question: A bank’s complaint-search table in pgvector holds 800,000 rows. What value of lists does pgvector suggest for an IVFFlat index?
quiz.explanation: Up to 1 million rows, pgvector suggests lists ≈ rows ÷ 1,000: 800,000 ÷ 1,000 = 800.

quiz.question: A brokerage embeds 16 million research-note chunks in pgvector. What value of lists is suggested?
quiz.explanation: Above 1 million rows the suggestion is √rows, and √16,000,000 = 4,000.

quiz.question: An IVFFlat product index had 0.96 recall at launch and now has 0.82. Which of these could explain the drop? Select all that apply.
options: Whole new product categories were added after the index was built
The index was built when the table held 5% of today’s rows
Many queries now fall near cluster borders
quiz.explanation: Stale centroids, unrepresentative training data and border queries all cost recall. Raising probes improves recall.

quiz.question: An IVF index over policy clauses has 2,500 lists. What starting value for probes does pgvector suggest?
quiz.explanation: Start probes around √lists: √2,500 = 50, then tune against measured recall.

quiz.question: 3 million merchant-description vectors sit in 3,000 lists of roughly equal size. With probes = 30, about how many vectors get exact distances per query?
quiz.explanation: Each list holds about 3,000,000 ÷ 3,000 = 1,000 vectors, and 30 lists × 1,000 = 30,000, or 1% of the data.

quiz.question: A hospital created an IVFFlat index on an empty table, then loaded 1.2 million note embeddings. Recall is very poor. What fixes it?
options: Rebuild the index now that representative data is loaded
Switch from cosine to L2 distance
Load more rows into the same index
quiz.explanation: IVF learns its centroids when the index is built. Built on no data, the clusters are meaningless until it is rebuilt.

quiz.question: What does “Flat” mean in IVFFlat?
options: The index has a single graph layer
Vectors inside each list are stored uncompressed, so distances within a list are exact
Every list has exactly the same size
The centroids are fixed and never trained
quiz.explanation: Flat means raw vectors in the lists. IVF-PQ is the variant that compresses them.

quiz.question: Which of these can be changed per query without rebuilding the index? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: probes, nprobe and ef_search are query-time settings. The number of lists is fixed when the index is trained.

quiz.question: A shipment-search index has recall@10 of 0.86 at probes = 10 against a 0.95 target, with latency to spare. What do you try first?
options: Rebuild with twice as many lists
Drop the index and use exact search
quiz.explanation: probes is the query-time recall dial. Rebuild only if the data has drifted from the centroids.

quiz.question: A developer sets probes equal to lists. What does the search become?
options: An exact scan of every vector, plus the centroid comparisons
A search over half the lists
A rebuild of the index at query time
quiz.explanation: Scanning every list means computing every distance, which is exact search with extra overhead.

quiz.question: A FAISS IVF index uses nlist = 4,096. FAISS warns when there are fewer than 39 training points per centroid. About how many training vectors do you need at minimum?
quiz.explanation: 39 × 4,096 = 159,744, so about 160,000 training vectors.

quiz.question: A bank builds an IVF index over 10 million transaction-narration embeddings. Which steps are sound? Select all that apply.
options: Train on a random sample rather than the first rows loaded
Build the index before loading any data, so inserts are fast
quiz.explanation: Centroids must be learned from representative data, and √rows is the suggested list count above 1 million rows.

quiz.question: A law firm stores 768-dimension float32 vectors in IVF-PQ with 64-byte codes. What is the compression factor inside the lists?
After a build on early data, the largest of 16 lists holds 40% of all vectors. A query that probes 2 lists including that one scans at least what share?
quiz.explanation: That one list alone holds 40% of the rows. Skewed lists make probing expensive, which is why you rebuild on representative data.

quiz.question: Why do queries near a cluster border need more probes?
options: Their true neighbours can sit in a neighbouring list that is not among the nearest centroids
The distance metric changes near borders
quiz.explanation: Choosing lists by centroid distance can skip the list that holds a neighbour just across the border.

quiz.question: When is IVFFlat a reasonable choice over HNSW? Select all that apply.
options: Fast index builds matter on a moderate dataset
Data is batch-loaded and the index is rebuilt nightly
Memory is tight and slightly lower recall is acceptable
Data arrives continuously and drifts, with no chance to rebuild
quiz.explanation: IVF builds quickly and uses little memory, but it depends on trained centroids, so drifting data favours HNSW.

quiz.question: 2 million vectors sit in 2,000 balanced lists and probes = 45. About how many vectors are scanned per query?
quiz.explanation: Each list holds about 1,000 vectors, so 45 lists × 1,000 = 45,000, which is 45 ÷ 2,000 = 2.25%.

quiz.question: A pgvector query filters to one circle (5% of rows) and uses IVFFlat with probes = 10. It returns 3 rows instead of 10. Why?
options: IVFFlat cannot be combined with a WHERE clause
The filter is applied after the probed lists are scanned, so few candidates match
quiz.explanation: Only about 5% of the scanned candidates survive the filter. Raise probes, or use iterative index scans in pgvector 0.8 and later.

quiz.question: What should you monitor after deploying an IVF index? Select all that apply.
options: Recall@10 against exact search on sample queries
The largest list’s share of rows
quiz.explanation: Recall, list balance and latency show when probes need tuning or the index needs rebuilding.

quiz.question: A learning platform on Postgres has 1.2 million lesson chunks and wants semantic search without running a new database. What fits?
options: pgvector with an IVFFlat or HNSW index
quiz.explanation: pgvector adds vector indexes next to existing tables and SQL filters, with no new system to run.
